reviewBoundary: Three whole-practice originals. Fictional class/workshop/email cases; same-author all-option and evidence review only, not student or teacher calibration.

units.title: A spare chair and a watching place
units.alignmentNote: Junior2 has two complete written four-question passages adapting the written-reading part of its level reference. Junior3 retains four emails with five questions and a separate five-question reading, all three-choice. Source supplies response structure, not prose.

materials.title: The spare chair
materials.text:
The drama club used our classroom on Friday afternoons. Every week, its members moved the desks to the sides and left a circle of chairs in the middle. On Monday, we had to arrange everything again before our first lesson.

I suggested drawing the desk positions on the floor with tape. Our teacher agreed to removable tape after checking that it would not damage the surface. We marked four corners of each group of desks, rather than drawing around every leg. The club could now return them without needing our class photograph.

The next Monday, the desks were right, but there was a chair in front of the cupboard. I wrote a sharp note asking the club not to leave furniture in the way. Before I put it up, my friend suggested asking why the chair was there.

A club member explained that an older visitor had come to talk about theatre. She needed a chair with arms, and the club had borrowed one from another room. They had left it near the cupboard for the caretaker to collect, but had forgotten to tell him.

We added one small box to our room checklist: borrowed furniture. The club would record where an extra item belonged and who was returning it. I kept my note in my bag. The problem needed a clearer handover, not a longer complaint. The room became easier to share once we explained the exceptions as well as the normal arrangement.

questions.prompt: Why did the class use removable tape?
options: To decorate the cupboard
To stop the club entering the room
To mark seats for a theatre show
To show where desk groups belonged
questions.explanation: Tape marks desk positions. It neither bars the club nor decorates storage or assigns audience seats.

questions.prompt: Why was the extra chair different?
options: The class had bought a new desk
It had been made from classroom tape
A visitor needed a chair with arms
The club wanted to block the cupboard
questions.explanation: The visitor required arms. The other accounts invent origins or intent.

questions.prompt: What had the club forgotten to do?
options: Remove all desks from the school
Draw every chair leg on the floor
Cancel its Friday meeting
Tell the caretaker about collecting the chair
questions.explanation: Collection needed a handover to the caretaker. Leg outlines were deliberately unnecessary, and no cancellation or school-wide removal was intended.

questions.prompt: What does the final checklist change address?
options: How to write a longer complaint
Who should act in the next play
The price of every desk
Items outside the usual room arrangement
questions.explanation: Borrowed furniture is an exception with a destination and return owner. Prices, complaint length and casting are not the checklist purpose.

materials.title: Watching without moving closer
materials.text:
Our class wanted to watch birds near the pond. The science teacher asked us to choose a place where we could see them without changing what they were doing. We selected a bench beside the path, well away from the water's edge.

On our first visit, two students walked towards a bird to get a larger photograph. The bird moved behind some plants. We could no longer see whether it had been eating or resting. The photograph was closer, but our observation had become less useful.

The next week, we stayed at the bench. Some students used binoculars, while others drew the shapes they could see. We agreed not to give the birds food to bring them nearer. We wanted to record their ordinary behaviour, not their response to our lunch.

At first, I wrote that a small brown bird was searching for insects. My partner asked what I had actually seen. It had turned several leaves over, but I had not seen what it picked up. I changed my note to describe the leaf-turning and placed my guess in a separate column.

Our report contained fewer confident names and explanations than I expected. It also contained clearer evidence. We could compare what happened on two visits without pretending we had understood every movement. Keeping our distance had helped in two ways: it gave the birds space, and it reminded us that watching something carefully is different from knowing everything about it.

questions.prompt: Why did the class choose the bench?
options: It was inside the pond
It guaranteed every bird would eat
It allowed observation at a distance
It provided free food for birds
questions.explanation: The bench gives a distant view. It is beside a path, and neither feeding nor guaranteed behaviour is promised.

questions.prompt: What happened when students approached one bird?
options: It moved out of clear view
It stayed exactly where it was
It began turning every leaf
It posed beside their lunch
questions.explanation: It went behind plants. The other actions are not reported in that episode.

questions.prompt: Why did the narrator change the note?
options: The note mixed a visible action with an unconfirmed explanation
The bird had eaten the written report
The partner had seen no leaves at all
The teacher required every bird to have a name
questions.explanation: Leaf-turning was observed; insect-searching was inferred. Neither absence of leaves, compulsory naming nor an eaten report explains the correction.

questions.prompt: What is the report described as having?
options: Only close photographs and no written notes
A complete explanation of all bird behaviour
Clearer evidence with some uncertainty retained
Proof that all birds eat the same food
questions.explanation: The final paragraph values evidence without complete knowledge. It explicitly lacks universal explanation and includes notes/drawings, not only photographs.

units.title: A music afternoon and a print maker

materials.title: Four messages about the music afternoon
materials.text:
From: Mrs Lee
Sent: Monday, 09:00
To: Student helpers
Subject: Saturday music afternoon
We expect twenty visitors at the community centre this Saturday. Please arrive at 13:00 to arrange chairs before doors open at 13:45. The demonstration begins at 14:00. Visitors may try the small percussion instruments afterwards. Please bring your helper badge; instruments and music stands will be provided. Let me know by Wednesday if you cannot come.

From: Arun
Sent: Tuesday, 16:20
To: Mrs Lee and student helpers
Subject: Re: Saturday music afternoon
I can help with the chairs, but I need to leave at 14:30. Would someone else collect the visitor feedback cards at the end? My sister can stay until everything is finished, but she is a visitor rather than a registered helper. I have not promised that she will do the job.

From: Mrs Lee
Sent: Wednesday, 10:15
To: Student helpers
Subject: Updated numbers and duties
There are now twenty-six visitors, so we need six more chairs. The times are unchanged. Kim has agreed to collect the feedback cards at 15:00. Arun, you can leave as planned. Thank you for checking the role before offering it to someone else. Visitors should be free to enjoy the afternoon without unexpected duties.

From: Kim
Sent: Friday, 17:10
To: Student helpers
Subject: Final reminder
The main entrance is being repaired. On Saturday, helpers and visitors should use the garden gate on Oak Street. I will put a sign there before 13:00. Badges are still needed. I have printed the feedback cards, so nobody else needs to bring copies. Please read Wednesday's visitor number when setting out the chairs; the number in Monday's message is no longer correct.

questions.prompt: How many visitor chairs should helpers set out?
options: Twenty
Twenty-six
Six
questions.explanation: Wednesday updates the total to26. Twenty is obsolete and six is only the increase.
Arrival remains13:00. 13:45 is visitor entry and15:00 feedback collection.

options: Arun’s sister
Arun after15:00
Kim
questions.explanation: Wednesday assigns Kim. The sister has no promised duty and Arun leaves14:30.

options: The entrance to use
The demonstration time
The requirement to wear badges
questions.explanation: It redirects entry to the garden gate. Times and badges remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: Why does Mrs Lee praise Arun’s check?
options: It allowed every helper to leave before the event
It increased the fee paid by his sister
It avoided assigning an unexpected job to a visitor
questions.explanation: The reply protects visitors from unagreed duties. Fees are absent and helpers are not all released early.

materials.title: The white parts of the picture
materials.text:
When I visited a print maker's workshop, I expected her to spend most of the time adding marks. Instead, she showed me how she removed parts of a soft printing block. The areas left raised would carry ink. The lower areas would stay white on the final paper.

She drew a simple tree on a practice block and asked me which part I would cut first. I pointed to its trunk. She invited me to think again: did I want a black trunk or a white one? I wanted it black. Cutting it away would produce the opposite result.

We made a pencil plan with the intended white areas shaded lightly, then checked it against the drawing. The shading was only a planning sign; it would not appear on the finished print. The artist completed the cutting while I watched from a safe position. This was a demonstration, not permission for an untrained visitor to use sharp tools.

After rolling ink over the raised surface, she pressed a sheet of paper onto it. The first print showed a small white break in one branch. I called it a mistake. She said it had not been in her plan, but she would examine it before deciding whether to alter the block. It might make the branch look lighter, or it might simply interrupt the shape.

The workshop changed how I looked at a printed picture. A blank area was not always an unfinished part waiting for more ink. Sometimes it was a deliberate shape made by removing material. I had been paying attention only to what was added, and missing half the decisions.

questions.prompt: Which parts of the block carry ink?
options: Only the deepest cuts
The raised parts
All parts below the surface
questions.explanation: Raised areas receive ink; cut areas remain white on paper.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator reconsider cutting the trunk?
options: The trunk should print black
The tree must have no trunk
The artist wants only white paper
questions.explanation: Removing it would make a white trunk, opposite the desired black trunk.

questions.prompt: What is the light pencil shading used for?
options: Showing where visitors may use tools alone
Planning which areas should be white
Adding colour to the final print
questions.explanation: The text explicitly calls it a plan sign, absent in the final print. It gives no independent tool authorization.

questions.prompt: How does the artist respond to the unplanned break?
options: She immediately destroys the entire block
She considers its effect before changing anything
She declares every accident successful
questions.explanation: She evaluates lightness versus interruption. She neither guarantees success nor destroys the work.

questions.prompt: What does the narrator learn about blank areas?
options: They always show unfinished work
They prove that no ink was used anywhere
They can be deliberate parts of a design
questions.explanation: The conclusion recognises intentional white shape. It rejects automatic incompleteness and the print uses ink.
